(Planning Dept.)
Recommendation :
It is recommended that the City Council:
(1)
Find that the Addendum to the 2015 Pasadena General Plan Environmental Impact
Report (State Clearinghouse No. 2013091009) to address the potential
environmental impacts associated with the
proposed amendments have been
prepared in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act of 1970
(CEQA) (Cal. Public Resources Code Section 21000, et. seq., as amended) and its
implementing
guidelines (Cal. Code Regs.,
Title 14, Section 15000 et. seq., 2016). This Addendum has been prepared and
will be processed consistent with CEQA Guidelines (Cal. Code Regs., Title 14,
Sections 15162 and
15164). The addendum found that
the proposed amendments will not result in any potentially significant impacts
that were not already analyzed;
(2)
Adopt the Findings for the Zoning Code Text Amendments (Attachment A of the
agenda report); and
(3)
Direct the City Attorney to prepare an ordinance for the Zoning Code Amendments
within 90 days consistent with the provisions set forth in the agenda report.
Recommendation of the Planning Commission :
On July 10, 2024, the Planning Commission considered
the proposed Zoning Code Amendments at a publicly noticed hearing and
recommended that the City
Council approve the Amendments
as presented by staff, with the following changes:
1.
Remove the maximum density limits for existing buildings. However, density
limits would apply to new construction with units;
2.
Require an average unit size of 450 square feet for projects with 10 or more
units. However, 100% affordable housing projects would be exempt;
3.
Reduce parking requirements when on-site car/vehicle sharing is provided; and
4.
Reduce open space requirements for properties in proximity to public parks.
The
Planning Commission made two additional recommendations that the City Council
direct staff to study at a future time:
1.
Whether adaptive reuse to housing should be allowed in zones that do not
currently allow housing (e.g., Industrial General and Commercial General zones);
and
2.
Financial incentives to facilitate adaptive reuse projects.

   CEREMONIAL MATTERS Mayor Gordo presented a proclamation declaring October 2024 as
  National Disability Employment Awareness Month, highlighted the
  importance of people with disabilities as vital parts of the community
  and he reaffirmed the City's commitment to inclusion and ensuring that
  City programs and employment practices effectively serve and benefit
  persons of all abilities. Marina Ovanessian, Acting Accessibility
  Coordinator, Valarie Struski, Vice Chair of the Accessibility and
  Disability Commission, and Chris Otera, Civitan President, thanked the
  City Council for the recognition and spoke on the significance of
  employment opportunities for those with all abilities, and the importance
  of inclusive workplaces to promote diversity and empowerment.

  Mayor Gordo presented a proclamation declaring October 2024 as
  Walktober and Pedestrian Safety Month, noting the benefits of walking
  as an active mode of transportation and the need for community safety
  and vigilance in maintaining pedestrian safety on the road. Joaquin
  Siques, Director of Transportation, Colin Bogart, Day One, and Tom
  Priestley, Pasadena Complete Streets Coalition, thanked the City
  Council for the recognition and invited the Council and community
  members to participate in Walktober events occurring throughout the
  month, with various opportunities to explore the City on foot.

  Mayor Gordo presented a proclamation declaring October 2024 as
  Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and reaffirmed the City's
  commitment to providing a community where no individual suffers the
  pain and hardships caused by the domestic violence. The Mayor
  thanked the City Prosecutor's Office for its efforts and advocacy on
  behalf of victims and working with local domestic violence service
  providers to prevent further abuses. City Attorney Bagneris accepted
  the proclamation on behalf of the community, introduced Jenna
  Monteilh, the City's newly hired Victim Witness Advocate, and thanked
  the City Council for authorizing this important position tasked with
  working on domestic violence cases. Tunisia Offray, Shepard's Door,
  also thanked the City Council for recognizing this important issue, the
  need to help victims recover and thrive, and spoke on how intervention
  and rehabilitation efforts create safer communities.

  PROGRAM

  Kris Markarian, Acting Public Works Director, provided introductory
  remarks on the item, and introduced Thanos Gauthier, Public Works
  Administrator, who presented information as part of a Powerpoint
  presentation on the City's Residential Organics Recycling program,
  providing background information on Senate Bill 1383, residential
u  organic waste collection, secured CalRecycle grants, compliance and
  enforcement efforts currently and upcoming, and community
  outreach/education efforts, and responded to questions.

  Council Minutes  2  09/30/2024
   In response to Councilmember Williams' inquiry regarding potentially
  eliminating the plastic bags used for securing organic scraps, Public
  Works Administrator Gauthier stated that after further research,
r  allowing the usage of plastic bags to secure and hold organic waste
  encourages more people to participate in the organics recycling
  program, and also reported that CalRecycle works directly with school
  districts on their recycling programs.

  In response to Councilmember Hampton's inquiry regarding the use of
  biodegradable bags, Public Works Administrator Gauthier stated that
  biodegradable bags are not accepted at the City's compost facility due
  to possible contamination caused by these types of bags, and also the
  premature disintegration of the bags limiting their usefulness in the
  separation process.

  Following discussion, on the order of the Mayor, and consensus of the
  City Council, the presentation was received and filed.

  Recommendation of the Planning Commission: On July 10, 2024,
  the Planning Commission considered the proposed Zoning Code
  Amendments at a publicly noticed hearing and recommended that the
  City Council approve the Amendments as presented by staff, with the
  following changes:
  1. Remove the maximum density limits for existing buildings.
  However, density limits would apply to new construction with units;
  2. Require an average unit size of 450 square feet for projects with

Council Minutes  5  09/30/2024
   3. Reduce parking requirements when on-site car/vehicle sharing is
  provided; and
  4. Reduce open space requirements for properties in proximity to
n  public parks.
  The Planning Commission made two additional recommendations that
  the City Council direct staff to study at a future time:
  1. Whether adaptive reuse to housing should be allowed in zones
  that do not currently allow housing (e.g., Industrial General and
  Commercial General zones); and
  2. Financial incentives to facilitate adaptive reuse projects.
  City Clerk Jomsky reported that the public hearing notice was published
  on September 16, 23, and 26, 2024 in the Pasadena Press, and that 3
  letters in support of the adaptive reuse concept and the proposed staff
  recommendations, including comments advocating for financial
  incentives to support the proposed ordinance and expanding the scope
  of beyond residential uses, were received by the City Clerk's Office,
  distributed to the City Council, posted online, and made part of the
  public record for this item.
  Jennifer Paige, Planning Director, provided introductory remarks on the
  item and introduced Melanie Hall, Planner, who presented a
  Powerpoint Presentation on adaptive reuse of existing non-residential
  buildings, and responded to questions.
  In response to Vice Mayor Madison's inquiry regarding instances in
  which the proposed amendments would not apply, Planning Director
  Paige stated that a building must have a certificate of occupancy for at
  least 5 years before becoming eligible for the adaptive reuse. She also
  noted that the residential impact fees, affordable housing requirements,
  inclusionary requirements, etc., will still apply upon conversion.
  Amanda Elioff, Pasadena resident, expressed support for the
  proposed adaptive reuse ordinance, but noted her concerns
  regarding the need for setbacks that are sensitive and compatible
  with adjacent neighbors.
  Ana Soutriver, residence not stated, expressed concerns that
  developers face significant financial costs when converting
  buildings, and advocated for the City to leverage financial tools to
  stimulate adaptive reuse and sustainable development.
  Elliot Gabay, West Hollywood resident, advocated to expand the
  adaptive reuse amendments beyond the scope of residential uses
  only.
